newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's new cosmodrome starts operation on Tuesday. [CORRECTED 09:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Russia's new cosmodrome starts operation on Tuesday. [CORRECTED 09:40 GMT]

text.p: Russia will stage the maiden launch from its new cosmodrome in the Far East on Tuesday when a military satellite blasts into orbit aboard a modified SS-25 ballistic missile, military space officials said.

The Svobodny cosmodrome, still being built on a former strategic nuclear missile base on the Siberian taiga 860 km (540 miles) west of Khabarovsk (corrects from "east of Khabarovsk"), is designed to reduce Russia's dependence on the main Soviet space centre at Baikonur, which Moscow now rents from independent Kazakhstan.

Colonel Sergei Gorbunov, a spokesman for Russia's Military Space Forces, said Svobodny -- the name means "Free" -- would become the main launch site for the commercial satellites Moscow is banking on to fund its financially troubled space industry.

The 87-kg (191 lb) Zeya military satellite, whose precise function has not been disclosed, will blast off at 0200 GMT on Tuesday aboard a Start booster rocket -- in effect a modified SS-25 Topol (Poplar) missile originally designed to carry nuclear payloads to North America.
Gorbunov said that a U.S. satellite, Early Bird, would be launched from Svobodny later this year. He gave no details.
Svobodny is sited on the same latitude as Baikonur and as such should allow much more effective launches than from Russia's two other sites in northern Russia.
"This will allow Russia to add to the full independence of its space programme," Gorbunov said. Moscow has had long squabbles with Kazakhstan over the maintenance and rent for Baikonur.

He said that Russia was also planning to launch heavy rockets from Svobodny but added that there were no immediate plans to transfer launches of manned space flights -- mainly those servicing the Mir space station.
Gorbunov said Svobodny, from which mainly solid-fuel rockets will be launched, posed no environmental dangers.
Nonetheless, those few people who live on the nearby taiga have been warned that bits of the booster rocket may fall back to earth during the launch.
